source.title: Classifying handedness in chiral nanomaterials using label error robust deep learning
source.authors: C. Groschner; Alexander J. Pattison; Assaf Ben-Moshe; A. Alivisatos; W. Theis; M. Scott

page_placements.theme: Selecting and correcting supervision can improve noisy-label performance

record.tranche_reason: Tests how controlled label error affects classification and test-set accuracy, using microscopy and MNIST data; it does not reproduce the original random-label training-error experiment.
record.gate_note: The study reports test accuracy on error-free test sets and minority-population estimates under increasing label error. It does not report training error or show that the networks fit the corrupted training labels perfectly. Several values are described in text but shown only as curves in figures.
record.test_reason: The study uses presumed early pattern learning and later memorization to motivate noise-robust training methods. Its results measure clean-test accuracy, class bias and population recovery, without measuring fitting or memorization of corrupted training labels. These robustness results do not establish V4's joint prediction of perfect training fit and progressively worse generalization.
record.authors_conclusion: The record is broadly accurate. The authors conclude that robustness depends on dataset features and correlations between label error and particle appearance. Two-step training and co-teaching improve robustness on idealized Te data, with two-step training giving more consistent population estimates; co-teaching performs best on as-synthesized data. Feature-complexity explanations and early-learning explanations are hypotheses, rather than directly measured mechanisms.
record.recipe_differences: Controlled label noise is created by mirroring a fraction of images and assigning labels; the study evaluates test classification and population recovery rather than fitting random labels and measuring chance test error.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome depends on dataset and label-error level; as-synthesized feature-correlated label error changes the relative performance of the methods. Co-teaching misclassification skew appears above 42% label error.

fits_no_version.finding: Standard CNN clean-test accuracy tolerates label error differently across datasets: accurate classification through 42% on MNIST sevens, but degradation after 10% on idealized Te images. Minority-population recovery remains accurate through 40% on idealized Te.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Generalization robustness to label noise depends on the dataset and its feature complexity.

fits_no_version.finding: Co-teaching and two-step training improve idealized Te classification robustness, with different class-bias and population-recovery behavior at high noise.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Noise mitigation methods differ in clean-test accuracy and population-estimation bias.

fits_no_version.finding: At 22% feature-correlated label error in as-synthesized Te data, clean-test accuracies are 0.65 ± 0.02 for standard CNN, 0.67 ± 0.03 for two-step training and 0.915 ± 0.003 for co-teaching.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Co-teaching outperforms the other tested methods on this practical noisy-label dataset.

record.problems: The study reports test accuracy but not training error, so it does not establish that corrupted training labels are fit perfectly. Several accuracy trends are described qualitatively from figures without exact values. Each method was trained three times; uncertainty is reported as standard error.
record.rows_left_out: No additional eligible results omitted. Figure-only numerical points were not reconstructed; textual trends and the Table 1 values are included.

untested.parts: Zero or near-zero training error under completely random labels, chance test performance, and unchanged training settings.
Relative training time and convergence speed as label corruption increases.
Training fit on shuffled, independently permuted or Gaussian-noise inputs.
Perfect corrupted-training-set fit alongside steady test degradation toward chance. Clean-test robustness is reported, but training fit and memorization are not.
Whether explicit regularization prevents random-label fitting and whether removing it impairs true-label generalization.
The temporal order of learning shared patterns and memorizing noisy labels; no corresponding training trajectories are measured.

record.verdict_notes: Do not interpret unreported training fit as failed training fit. The Methods specify label-error generation from 0% to 50%; in balanced binary classification, 50% random flips corresponds to chance labels. That endpoint alone does not establish random-label memorization. All extracted rows concern robustness or method performance and should not remain main evidence rows for these versions.

versions.untested_parts: No completely random labeling condition or training-error result; the study uses controlled mirror-generated label error and reports test performance.
Does not report training time or convergence speed by label-error fraction.
Does not test shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.

Does not report whether training error remains perfect; label error is tested from 0% to near 50%, not all labels corrupted. Test performance is measured on the study's image datasets, not as a general result for standard deep networks.
Does not compare removing weight decay, dropout, or data augmentation, or test generalization on true labels after removing them.
Does not measure the order in which true patterns and noisy labels are learned during training.

rows.subject: standard CNN
rows.operation_detail: Trained on MNIST seven images with controlled label error; evaluated on error-free ground-truth test set.
rows.value: Can learn the classes accurately up to 42% label error.
rows.uncertainty: Standard error across three separately trained networks; figure values not stated.
rows.note: The text gives a qualitative upper range; exact accuracy values are figure-only. Training-set error is not reported.
rows.check: Clean-test accuracy through 42% label error measures noise robustness; it does not show whether the CNN fits erroneous training labels.

rows.subject: standard CNN
rows.operation_detail: Trained on Te SEM images with controlled label error; evaluated on error-free ground-truth test set.
rows.value: Accuracy begins to degrade after 10% label error; reasonable accuracy is recovered up to 30% label error.
rows.uncertainty: Standard error across three separately trained networks; figure values not stated.
rows.locator: Results, “Application to idealized datasets of Te chiral nanoparticles”; Fig. 4a
rows.note: Text describes the trend and ranges, but not exact accuracy values. Training-set error is not reported.
rows.check: Declining clean-test accuracy alone does not establish V4's memorization-with-degradation effect; training fit is unreported.

rows.subject: standard CNN
rows.operation_detail: Trained on Te SEM images with controlled label error; tested for recovery of minority population fraction.
rows.value: Able to accurately predict the fraction of the minority population up to 40% label error.
rows.locator: Results, “Application to idealized datasets of Te chiral nanoparticles”; Fig. 4c
rows.note: This measures population estimation, not training error.
rows.check: Minority-population recovery measures aggregate prediction accuracy, not fitting corrupted labels or the training/test relationship in V4.

rows.subject: co-teaching method (two identical CNNs)
rows.operation_detail: Trained with co-teaching on Te SEM images with controlled label error; evaluated on error-free ground-truth test set.
rows.value: From 0% to approximately 40% label error the recovered accuracy is very consistent; accuracy is dramatically reduced beyond 40%.
rows.uncertainty: Standard error across three separately trained networks; figure values not stated.
rows.locator: Results, “Application to idealized datasets of Te chiral nanoparticles”; Fig. 4a
rows.note: At very low label error the standard CNN achieves higher accuracy; the co-teaching method performs better as label error increases past 10%.
rows.check: This is performance of a mitigation method that filters training examples. Neither full corrupted-set fit nor memorization is measured.

rows.subject: co-teaching method (two identical CNNs)
rows.operation_detail: Trained with co-teaching on Te SEM images with controlled label error; assessed class-specific errors.
rows.value: The network appears to be significantly over-predicting left-handed particles.
rows.locator: Results, “Application to idealized datasets of Te chiral nanoparticles”; Fig. 4b
rows.note: The text reports the direction of the skew but gives no exact values.
rows.check: Class-specific prediction bias under co-teaching does not measure any version. The source also describes over-predicting left-handed particles here but underestimating minority left-handed particles in its discussion of Fig. 4c; this directional inconsistency should be retained as unresolved.

rows.subject: co-teaching method (two identical CNNs)
rows.operation_detail: Trained with co-teaching on Te SEM images with controlled label error; tested for recovery of minority population fraction.
rows.value: Badly underestimate[s] the number of minority handed particles past 42% label error.
rows.locator: Results, “Application to idealized datasets of Te chiral nanoparticles”; Fig. 4c
rows.note: Text describes the direction and range, without exact values.
rows.check: Population underestimation under a mitigation method does not measure fitting corrupted training labels.

rows.subject: two-step training method
rows.operation_detail: Pretrained on a tiny error-free set, then trained on Te SEM images with controlled label error; evaluated on error-free ground-truth test set.
rows.value: Performs well up to about 40% label error; standard CNN and co-teaching sometimes slightly outperform it in accuracy.
rows.uncertainty: Standard error across three separately trained networks; figure values not stated.
rows.locator: Results, “Application to idealized datasets of Te chiral nanoparticles”; Fig. 4a
rows.note: The authors describe the two-step method as among the approaches sustaining high accuracy with more than 40% label error elsewhere in the discussion; this result's stated range is about 40%.
rows.check: Clean-test accuracy after supervised pretraining measures the proposed method's robustness. It does not measure memorization or learning order.
